question.explanation:
We note that $m = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $2m$ and $3m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

\[ \textrm{LCM}(2m, 3m) = 6m. \]

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6m,$ and simplify:

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \dfrac{3m+2}{2m} - \dfrac{m+2}{3m} &= 1\\[5pt] 6m\cdot \left(\dfrac{3m+2}{2m} - \dfrac{m+2}{3m}\right) &= 6m\cdot \left(1\right)\\[5pt] 6m\cdot \dfrac{3m+2}{2m} -6m\cdot \dfrac{m+2}{3m} &= 6m\cdot 1 \\[5pt] 3\cdot \cancel{2m}\cdot \dfrac{3m+2}{\cancel{2m}} -2\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot \dfrac{m+2}{\cancel{3m}} &= 6m \\[5pt] 3(3m+2) -2(m+2) &= 6m \end{align*}

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

\begin{align*} 3(3m+2) -2(m+2) &= 6m \\[3pt] 9m+6-2m-4&=6m \\[3pt] 7m+2&=6m \\[3pt] m &= -2 \end{align*}

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=-2\neq 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=-2.$

example.title: Solving Rational Equations Containing Two Distinct Linear Denominators

question.explanation:
We note that $x = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $x^2$ and $x.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

\[ \textrm{LCM}(x^2, x) = x^2. \]

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $x^2,$ and simplify:

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \dfrac{x-4}{x^2} - \dfrac{1}{x^2} &= \dfrac {2}{x} \\[5pt] x^2\cdot \left(\dfrac{x-4}{x^2} - \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) &= x^2\cdot \left(\dfrac {2}{x}\right) \\[5pt] x^2\cdot \left(\dfrac{x-4}{x^2}\right) - x^2\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) &= x^2\cdot \left(\dfrac {2}{x}\right) \\[5pt] \cancel{x^2}\cdot \left(\dfrac{x-4}{\cancel{x^2}}\right) - \cancel{x^2}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{\cancel{x^2}}\right) &=x\cdot \cancel{x}\cdot \left(\dfrac {2}{\cancel{x}}\right) \\[5pt] (x-4) - 1 &= 2x \end{align*}

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

\begin{align*} (x-4) - 1 &= 2x \\[3pt] x-5 &= 2x \\[3pt] x &= -5 \end{align*}

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=-5\neq 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=-5.$

example.title: Solving Rational Equations Containing Quadratic Denominators

question.explanation:
We note that $w = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $2w$ and $3w.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that \[ \textrm{LCM}(2w, 3w) = 6w. \]

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6w,$ and simplify: \[ \require{cancel} \eqalign{ \dfrac{4-w} {3w} + \dfrac{2w-1} {2w} &= \dfrac {2} {3}\\[5pt] 6w\cdot\left(\dfrac{4-w} {3w} + \dfrac{2w-1} {2w}\right) &= 6w\cdot\left(\dfrac {2} {3}\right) \\[5pt] 6w\cdot \left(\dfrac{4-w} {3w}\right) + 6w\cdot \left(\dfrac{2w-1} {2w}\right) &= 6w\cdot\dfrac {2} {3}\\[5pt] 2\cdot\cancel{3w}\cdot\left(\dfrac{4-w}{\cancel{3w}}\right) + 3\cdot\cancel{2w}\cdot\left(\dfrac{2w-1}{\cancel{2w}}\right) &= 2\cdot\cancel{3}\cdot w\cdot\dfrac {2}{\cancel{3}} \\[5pt] 2(4-w) + 3 (2w-1) &= 4w } \]

We now have a linear equation in $w,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles: \begin{align*} 2(4-w) + 3 (2w-1) &= 4w \\[3pt] 8-2w+6w-3 &= 4w \\[3pt] 5 &= 4w-4w \\[3pt] 5 &=0, \end{align*} which is a false statement. Therefore, we conclude that there is no solution.

example.title: Solving Rational Equations Containing Two Distinct Linear Denominators

question.explanation:
We note that $w = 0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

The equation has the denominators $2w, 3w,$ and $9w.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\textrm{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

\[ \textrm{LCM}(2w, 3w, 9w) = 18w. \]

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $18w,$ and simplify:

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \dfrac{2w-3}{3w} &= \dfrac{1-w}{2w} - \dfrac{4w-1}{9w}\\[5pt] 18w\cdot\left(\dfrac{2w-3}{3w}\right) &= 18w\cdot\left(\dfrac{1-w}{2w} - \dfrac{4w-1}{9w}\right)\\[5pt] 18w\cdot\left( \dfrac{2w-3}{3w}\right) &= 18w\cdot \left(\dfrac{1-w}{2w}\right) + 18w\cdot \left(-\dfrac{4w-1}{9w}\right)\\[5pt] 6\cdot3w\cdot\left( \dfrac{2w-3}{3w}\right) &= 9\cdot 2w\cdot \left(\dfrac{1-w}{2w}\right) - 2\cdot 9w\cdot \left(\dfrac{4w-1}{9w}\right)\\[5pt] 6\cdot\cancel{3w}\cdot\left( \dfrac{2w-3}{\cancel{3w}}\right) &= 9\cdot \cancel{2w}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1-w}{\cancel{2w}}\right) - 2\cdot \cancel{9w}\cdot \left(\dfrac{4w-1}{\cancel{9w}}\right)\\[5pt] 6\cdot (2w-3) &=9\cdot (1-w) - 2\cdot (4w-1) \end{align*}

We now have a linear equation in $w,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

\begin{align*} 6(2w-3) &= 9(1-w) - 2(4w-1)\\[5pt] 12w-18 &= 9-9w-8w+2 \\[5pt] 12w-18 &= 11-17w \\[5pt] 12w+17w &=11+18 \\[5pt] 29w &=29 \\[5pt] w &= 1 \end{align*}

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $w=0$ as a solution. But since $w=1\neq 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $w=1.$
